Prescribe 40-mg prednisone daily for 14 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the presence of a linear depression along a superficial vein, visible when the forearm is raised, which is characteristic of eosinophilic fasciitis. Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis was diagnosed based on the patient’s history, venous groove sign, and characteristic findings on MRI. After 1 month of treatment with oral prednisone (40 mg daily), she gained 4.54 kg (10 lb), so oral methotrexate (20 mg weekly) with folic acid (1 mg daily) was initiated, and the prednisone dose was tapered over 3 months. She underwent physical therapy twice weekly and was advised to take oral calcium (1000 mg daily) and vitamin D (1000 IU daily) due to concerns about adverse effects on bone associated with steroid use and to use contraception due to potential teratogenicity of methotrexate. At most recent follow-up 6 months after initial presentation, the skin tightening on her bilateral forearms and shins had decreased and her hand and elbow mobility had improved, but the groove sign on the right forearm persisted.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis
